subjective.question: Differentiate between impairment and depreciation.
subjective.answer: Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of an asset over its estimated useful life. Depreciation for the accounting period is charged to the profit and loss account for the period, either directly or indirectly. Impairment, on the other hand, is a fall in the value of an asset due to reasons beyond the control of the company, so that its recoverable amount becomes less than its carrying value in the balance sheet. While depreciation is a planned, systematic charge, impairment is an unplanned write-down of the asset to its recoverable amount.

subjective.question: What is the difference between authorized capital and paid-up capital?
subjective.answer: Authorized Capital: It is the maximum limit of the amount of capital that a company can issue, as mentioned in the Memorandum and Articles of Association of the company. A company cannot issue capital exceeding this amount unless it amends its Memorandum and Articles of Association. Paid-up Capital: It is the amount of capital that the company actually issues out of the authorized capital and which has been paid up by the shareholders. The minimum amount of capital that a company can issue is one share each for each of its members, and the maximum is equal to the authorized capital. A company can issue shares of different classes having different denominations and different rights attached to them.

subjective.question: A partially completed inventory item is held at the year end. Its expected selling price when completed is Rs. 2,500, a further cost of Rs. 500 is required to complete it, and the expected selling cost is Rs. 100. What will be the carrying value of the item if the cost incurred to date is (i) Rs. 1,000, (ii) Rs. 1,900 and (iii) Rs. 2,100?
subjective.answer: Net Realizable Value (NRV) of the item = Selling price - Selling expenses - Completion costs = 2,500 - 100 - 500 = Rs. 1,900. Inventory is carried at the lower of cost and NRV: (i) Cost Rs. 1,000 vs NRV Rs. 1,900: Cost is less than NRV, therefore the inventory will be shown at cost (Rs. 1,000) and no adjustment is required. (ii) Cost Rs. 1,900 vs NRV Rs. 1,900: Cost is equal to NRV, therefore the inventory will be shown at cost (Rs. 1,900) and no adjustment is required. (iii) Cost Rs. 2,100 vs NRV Rs. 1,900: Cost is greater than NRV, therefore the inventory will be shown at NRV (Rs. 1,900) and written down by Rs. 200.

subjective.question: Differentiate between the benchmark treatment and the allowed alternative treatment of borrowing costs under IAS 23.
subjective.answer: Benchmark Treatment: The benchmark treatment of borrowing costs is the most straightforward and prudent. Under it, borrowing costs should be treated as an expense in the period in which they are incurred, regardless of how the loan is used. If the benchmark treatment is used, the enterprise is only required to disclose the accounting policy adopted for borrowing costs. Allowed Alternative Treatment: Under the allowed alternative treatment, borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset may be capitalized as part of the cost of that asset. Any other borrowing costs remaining must still be recognized as an expense, as under the benchmark treatment. The standard lays down the criteria for determining which borrowing costs are eligible for capitalization.

subjective.question: Write down the types of stocks for trading and manufacturing concerns.
subjective.answer: Different types of businesses have different types of inventories: Trading concerns: - Stock in Trade (finished inventory only) Manufacturing concerns: - Raw Material - Work in Process - Finished Goods

subjective.question: Trade debts considered good - unsecured are Rs. 11,000 and trade debts considered doubtful - unsecured are Rs. 41,000. The provision for doubtful debts is Rs. 41,000. Show this information in the notes to the accounts under the head of Trade Debts (Current Assets).
subjective.answer: TRADE DEBTS Considered good - unsecured: Rs. 11,000 Considered doubtful - unsecured: Rs. 41,000 Less: Provision for doubtful debts: (Rs. 41,000) Total trade debts shown in current assets: Rs. 11,000

subjective.question: Define current liabilities. What heads should be included in current liabilities? Also give the heads of long-term liabilities.
subjective.answer: Current liabilities are all those liabilities that are expected to be paid, or will become due for payment, within 12 months from the balance sheet date. Current liabilities may include any or all of the following heads: - Trade and other payables - Interest, profit, return or mark-up accrued on loans and other payables - Short term borrowings - Current portion of long term borrowings - Current portion of long term murabaha - Provision for taxation Long-term liabilities are all those liabilities that will become due for payment after a period of 12 months from the balance sheet date. They may include: - Long term financing - Debentures - Liabilities against assets subject to finance lease - Long term modaraba - Long term deposits - Deferred liabilities

subjective.question: What is the difference between the LIFO and FIFO methods of inventory valuation?
subjective.answer: Under the LIFO (Last In, First Out) method, the basic assumption is that the most recently purchased units are sold first and the older units remain in inventory. This assumption is not in accord with the physical flow of merchandise in most businesses. Under LIFO, the costs assigned to cost of goods sold are relatively current, because they stem from the most recent purchases. Under the FIFO (First In, First Out) method, the oldest purchase costs are transferred to cost of goods sold, while the most recent costs remain in inventory. When purchase costs are rising, the FIFO method assigns lower (older) costs to cost of goods sold and the higher, more recent costs to the goods remaining in inventory, resulting in a higher reported profit and a higher closing inventory value than LIFO.

subjective.question: Describe the going concern assumption.
subjective.answer: The going concern concept implies that the business will continue to operate for the foreseeable future. It is assumed that the entity has neither the intention nor the need to liquidate or curtail its operations. The effect of the going concern assumption is that the assets and liabilities of the business are meant to be held till their maturity (or useful life to the business) and are therefore measured and reported at their cost. If the business is not considered to be a going concern, then the assets and liabilities would have to be shown at their current market value.

subjective.question: A company has an asset which originally cost Rs. 1,250,000. It was revalued upwards to Rs. 1,750,000 two years ago. The value has now fallen to Rs. 140,000. Pass the adjustment entry for the fall in value.
subjective.answer: The total fall in value is Rs. 1,750,000 - Rs. 140,000 = Rs. 1,610,000. Out of this, Rs. 500,000 is adjusted against the existing revaluation surplus (Rs. 1,750,000 - Rs. 1,250,000) and the remaining Rs. 1,110,000 is charged to the income statement. The double entry is: Debit: Revaluation Surplus - Rs. 500,000 Debit: Income and Expense Account - Rs. 1,110,000 Credit: Asset Value (Balance Sheet) - Rs. 1,610,000

subjective.question: What type of information must be disclosed separately on the face of the financial statements when the equity method is used for the recognition of investment in associates?
subjective.answer: Investments made for a long term are recorded using the equity method and shown separately in the balance sheet as long-term assets. Investments made for a short period of time are recognized at cost and classified as short-term investments. Under the equity method, the investment is initially recorded at cost and the carrying amount is increased or decreased to recognize the investor's share of the profit or loss of the investee after the date of acquisition, and the investor's share is disclosed separately in the financial statements.

subjective.question: Differentiate between bad debts and doubtful debts.
subjective.answer: Bad debts: When debtors fail to settle their accounts for items sold on credit, a bad debt occurs. A bad debt is an amount written off by the business as a loss and classified as an expense, because the debt owed to the business cannot be collected and all reasonable efforts to collect it have been exhausted. The debt is immediately written off by crediting the debtor's account, eliminating any balance remaining in that account. Doubtful debts: Doubtful debts are those debts which a business is unlikely to be able to collect. The reasons for potential non-payment can include disputes over supply, delivery and condition of goods, or the appearance of financial stress within a customer's operations. When such a dispute occurs, it is prudent to add this debt, or a portion thereof, to the doubtful debt reserve (provision for doubtful debts). This is done to avoid over-stating the assets of the business, as trade debtors are reported net of the provision for doubtful debts.

subjective.question: What qualitative characteristics make financial information useful?
subjective.answer: The financial statements should possess the following qualitative characteristics: - Understandability - Relevance - Materiality - Reliability - Faithful representation - Substance over form - Neutrality - Prudence - Completeness - Comparability - Timeliness - Balance between cost and benefit - Balance between qualitative characteristics - True and fair presentation

subjective.question: What information is to be disclosed for the classes of share capital?
subjective.answer: Share capital shall be classified under the following sub-heads: Issued, subscribed and paid-up capital, distinguishing in respect of each class between: (a) Shares allotted for consideration paid in cash; (b) Shares allotted for consideration other than cash, showing separately shares issued against property and others (to be specified); and (c) Shares allotted as bonus shares.

subjective.question: Differentiate between the periodic and perpetual inventory systems.
subjective.answer: Perpetual Inventory System: - Receipt of inventory is debited to the Stock Account. - Issues are credited to the Stock Account and debited to the Material Consumption Account. - Value is assigned to every issue according to the selected valuation policy. - The Material Consumption Account becomes part of the Trading Account or Work in Process Account. Periodic Inventory System: - Receipt of inventory is debited to the Purchases Account. - No recording is made for individual issues in the General Ledger. - The available balance of stock in trade at the end of the period is valued according to the selected policy, and closing stock is recorded by debiting the Stock Account and crediting the Trading Account or Work in Process Account.

subjective.question: What are financial assets? Explain the measurement bases used in financial statements.
subjective.answer: Financial assets are recognized when the company becomes a party to the contractual provisions of the instrument. The particular measurement methods adopted are disclosed in the individual policy statements associated with each item. The measurement bases used in financial statements are: - Historical cost: The consideration paid (payable) or received (receivable) at the time of recording the transaction, with no relation to current costs. - Current cost: The consideration that would have to be paid if the same or an equivalent asset is acquired currently. - Realizable value: The consideration that would be realized by selling an asset in an orderly disposal. - Settlement value: The undiscounted amounts of cash or cash equivalents expected to be paid to satisfy the liabilities in the normal course of business. - Present value: A current estimate of the present discounted value of the future net cash flows in the normal course of business. Historical cost is the most commonly adopted measurement basis, but it is usually combined with other bases, e.g. inventory is carried at the lower of cost and net realizable value.

subjective.question: Write down the components of the IASB Framework.
subjective.answer: The Framework consists of several sections, which are as follows: - The Objective of Financial Statements - Underlying Assumptions - Qualitative Characteristics of Financial Statements - The Elements of Financial Statements - Recognition of the Elements of Financial Statements - Measurement of the Elements of Financial Statements - Concepts of Capital and Capital Maintenance

subjective.question: What is meant by significant influence?
subjective.answer: Significant influence is the ability to participate in, but not to control, the financial and management (operating) policy decisions of an enterprise. As per IAS 28, an investor is presumed to have significant influence over the investee if the investor holds twenty percent (20%) or more of the voting power in the investee.

subjective.question: What are the disclosure requirements for long-term loans and advances?
subjective.answer: The following information must be disclosed in the financial statements in the case of long-term loans and advances (they shall also be classified as secured and unsecured): amounts considered good, doubtful and bad, distinguishing between: - Loans and advances to subsidiary companies, controlled firms, managed modarabas and other associated companies; - Loans and advances to the chief executive, directors and executives of the company; and - Other loans and advances.

subjective.question: Explain the straight line method and the reducing balance method of depreciation, with the help of an example.
subjective.answer: Straight Line Method: This method depreciates cost evenly throughout the useful life of the fixed asset. Straight line depreciation is calculated as follows: Depreciation per annum = (Cost - Residual Value) / Useful Life Reducing Balance Method: This method charges depreciation at a higher rate in the earlier years of an asset, and the amount of depreciation reduces as the life of the asset progresses. It is calculated as follows: Depreciation per annum = (Net Book Value - Residual Value) x Rate% Example: An asset has a useful life of 3 years, cost of $2,000, residual value of $500 and a depreciation rate of 50%. Year 1: (2,000 - 500) x 50% = 750; Accumulated depreciation = 750 Year 2: (1,250 - 500) x 50% = 375; Accumulated depreciation = 1,125 Year 3: 375 (adjusted in the final year so that the asset is written down to its residual value); Accumulated depreciation = 1,500 Total depreciation over the life of the asset = Cost - Residual Value = 2,000 - 500 = 1,500.

subjective.question: What is the main objective of the preparation of financial statements?
subjective.answer: The objective of financial statements is to provide information about the financial position, performance and changes in financial position of an entity that is useful to a wide range of users in making economic decisions. Such financial statements meet the needs of most users. The information is, however, restricted because: - It is based on past events, not expected future events; and - It does not necessarily contain non-financial information.

subjective.question: How many types of relations exist among different companies?
subjective.answer: Two or more companies may be interconnected or interrelated in one of the following manners: - They can have a business relationship of such a nature that they can be termed as Related Parties. - They can be Associated to each other. - One company can be a subsidiary of the other.

subjective.question: Who is responsible for the preparation and maintenance of the financial statements of a company?
subjective.answer: - It is the responsibility of the directors of every company to prepare the annual accounts of the company. - Directors of every company should lay before the Annual General Meeting a Balance Sheet and a Profit and Loss Account or Income and Expenditure Account, as the case may be. - The first annual accounts of the company will be prepared within eighteen (18) months of the incorporation of the company. - Subsequently, annual accounts will be prepared every year. - In addition, listed companies are required to prepare quarterly and half yearly accounts.

subjective.question: What is the effect of revaluation of an asset and how is it adjusted?
subjective.answer: The value of an item of property, plant and equipment may be increased or decreased as a result of revaluation. IAS 16 requires the increase to be credited to a revaluation surplus (i.e. part of owners' equity), unless the increase is reversing a previous decrease which was recognized as an expense. To the extent that this offset is made, the increase is recognized as income; any excess is then taken to the revaluation reserve. A revaluation loss (decrease) is charged to the profit and loss account in the period in which the revaluation is carried out. However, a revaluation decrease should be charged directly against any related revaluation surplus to the extent that the decrease does not exceed the amount held in surplus in respect of the same asset.

subjective.question: Explain the different types of financial risks that an entity may assume or transfer to another party while undertaking transactions in financial instruments.
subjective.answer: In undertaking transactions in financial instruments, an entity may assume or transfer to another party one or more of the following types of financial risk: - Market risk: It includes (i) Currency risk - the risk that the value of a financial instrument will fluctuate due to changes in foreign exchange rates; (ii) Interest rate risk - the risk that the value of a financial instrument will fluctuate due to changes in market interest rates; and (iii) Price risk - the risk that the value of a financial instrument will fluctuate due to changes in market prices, whether caused by factors specific to the individual instrument or its issuer, or factors affecting all securities traded in the market. - Credit risk: The risk that one party to a financial instrument will fail to discharge an obligation and cause the other party to incur a financial loss. - Liquidity risk: The risk that an entity will encounter difficulty in raising funds to meet commitments associated with financial instruments. It may result from an inability to sell a financial asset quickly at close to its fair value. - Cash flow / interest rate risk: The risk that the future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of changes in market interest rates. In the case of a floating rate debt instrument, such fluctuations result in a change in the effective interest rate of the financial instrument, usually without a corresponding change in its fair value.

subjective.question: Differentiate between a public listed company and a public unlisted company.
subjective.answer: A public listed company is a public company whose shares are listed (quoted) on a stock exchange and can be freely bought and sold by the general public. It has to comply with the listing regulations of the stock exchange and the additional disclosure and reporting requirements of the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan, including quarterly and half yearly accounts. A public unlisted company is a public company whose shares are not listed on any stock exchange. Although it can offer its shares to the public, its shares are not traded on a stock exchange, and it is not subject to the listing regulations, though it remains subject to the requirements of the Companies Ordinance 1984 applicable to public companies.

subjective.question: Describe a private company.
subjective.answer: A private company is a company which, by its articles of association: - Restricts the right to transfer its shares; - Limits the number of its members to fifty (50), excluding persons who are in the employment of the company; and - Prohibits any invitation to the public to subscribe for any shares in, or debentures of, the company. A private company enjoys certain privileges and exemptions under the Companies Ordinance 1984 as compared to a public company, and it uses the words '(Private) Limited' at the end of its name.

subjective.question: Enlist any five heads of current assets under the Fourth Schedule of the Companies Ordinance 1984.
subjective.answer: Under the Fourth Schedule of the Companies Ordinance 1984, current assets include the following heads: - Stock in trade - Trade debts - Loans and advances - Trade deposits and short term prepayments - Other receivables - Short term investments - Cash and bank balances (Any five of the above.)

subjective.question: Briefly explain trade discount and cash discount.
subjective.answer: Trade discount is a reduction in the list price of goods allowed by a seller to a buyer at the time of sale, usually for bulk purchases or trade customers. It is not recorded in the books of account; the purchase or sale is recorded at the net amount after deducting trade discount. Cash discount is a reduction in the amount payable allowed by a seller to a buyer for prompt payment within a specified period. Unlike trade discount, cash discount is recorded in the books of account: the buyer records it as discount received and the seller records it as discount allowed.

subjective.question: Discuss intangible assets with examples.
subjective.answer: An intangible asset is an identifiable non-monetary asset without physical substance. It is identifiable when it is separable from the entity or arises from contractual or legal rights. Examples of intangible assets include goodwill, patents, copyrights, trademarks, licences, franchises and computer software. Under IAS 38, an intangible asset is recognized only if it is probable that the future economic benefits attributable to the asset will flow to the entity and the cost of the asset can be measured reliably. Internally generated goodwill is never recognized as an asset. Intangible assets are initially measured at cost and are subsequently carried at cost less accumulated amortization and impairment losses, or under the revaluation model where an active market exists.

subjective.question: Opening stock is Rs. 15,000, closing stock is Rs. 30,000 and the cost of direct material consumed is Rs. 45,000. Calculate the amount of purchases.
subjective.answer: Cost of direct material consumed = Opening stock + Purchases - Closing stock 45,000 = 15,000 + Purchases - 30,000 Purchases = 45,000 - 15,000 + 30,000 Purchases = Rs. 60,000

subjective.question: List down the procedure adopted for the formation of a company in Pakistan.
subjective.answer: The procedure for the formation of a company in Pakistan is as follows: 1. Availability of name: An application is made to the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) to check and reserve the availability of the proposed name of the company, so that it is not identical to the name of an existing company. 2. Preparation of documents: The Memorandum of Association and Articles of Association are prepared and printed. 3. Filing of documents: The Memorandum and Articles of Association, along with the prescribed forms (declaration of compliance, particulars of directors, address of the registered office, etc.) are filed with the Registrar of Companies / SECP together with the prescribed filing fee, which depends on the authorized capital. 4. Certificate of Incorporation: On satisfaction, the Registrar issues the Certificate of Incorporation, from which date the company comes into existence as a separate legal entity. 5. Certificate of Commencement of Business: A public company must additionally obtain a certificate of commencement of business before it can start its business operations.

subjective.question: Define contingent liability as per IAS 37.
subjective.answer: As per IAS 37, a contingent liability is: (a) A possible obligation that arises from past events and whose existence will be confirmed only by the occurrence or non-occurrence of one or more uncertain future events not wholly within the control of the entity; or (b) A present obligation that arises from past events but is not recognized because it is not probable that an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation, or the amount of the obligation cannot be measured with sufficient reliability. A contingent liability is not recognized in the balance sheet; it is only disclosed in the notes to the financial statements, unless the possibility of an outflow of resources is remote.
